_note: Evergreen weekly series. Wednesday = explained, Thursday = buysmart; one topic per week, rotating. 'kw' must match a watchlist keyword to show its live 8-week chart on the cover. Review quarterly (prices, retailers, rules). No medical claims.

explained.title: PDRN, explained: the 'salmon DNA' ingredient Korea made famous
explained.sub: Why Korean clinics and drugstores are full of it, and what it actually is.
points: Polydeoxyribonucleotide: purified DNA fragments, traditionally from salmon. Plant-based versions now exist too.
In Korea it was a dermatology-clinic treatment first, best known through skin-booster injections, before it moved into everyday serums and creams.
It is marketed for recovering, calmer-looking skin after treatments, sun or stress. Topical results vary by formula.
Look for where PDRN sits in the ingredient list and whether the source is salmon or plant. Patch-test first, like any new active.

explained.title: Cica, explained: the Korean answer to irritated skin
explained.sub: Centella asiatica is in thousands of Korean products. Here is why.
points: Cica comes from centella asiatica, a plant traditionally used on skin. Korean labels call it 'cica'.
Look for madecassoside, asiaticoside and madecassic acid on the label: these are the plant's main actives.
It became the default 'soothing' ingredient for redness-prone and post-treatment skin, so most brands carry a cica line.
'Cica' on the front can mean very little inside. Check that centella actives appear high in the ingredient list.

explained.title: Toner pads, explained: why every Korean bathroom has a jar
explained.sub: A Korean staple that is still unfamiliar in most markets.
points: Cotton or fabric pads pre-soaked in toner, sold in a jar of 60 to 100 with tweezers.
Wipe after cleansing to remove leftovers and prep skin, or leave one on a dry spot for a few minutes as a mini mask.
Exfoliating (with AHA, BHA or PHA), soothing (cica, heartleaf) and brightening pads. They are not interchangeable.
Exfoliating pads daily can be too much for sensitive skin. Start every other day.

explained.title: Buldak, explained: the noodle that made spicy go global
explained.sub: How hot it really is, and how Koreans actually eat it.
points: 'Buldak' means fire chicken. Samyang's stir-fried noodles launched in 2012 and turned spicy challenges into a global trend.
Carbonara, cheese and cream versions are milder; the original and 2x spicy are the hottest. Heat differs a lot by flavour.
With cheese, mayo, a fried egg or rice to soften the heat, and often with a cold drink or milk on the side.
Check each flavour's heat on the pack and whether the version is made for your market; ingredient lists can differ by country.

explained.title: Gochujang, explained: Korea's essential red chilli paste
explained.sub: The flavour behind tteokbokki, bibimbap and much more.
points: A fermented paste of chilli powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybean and salt. Sweet, savoury and spicy at once.
Most tubs show a heat level on the label, from mild to very hot. Start mild.
Stir into stews and sauces, mix with vinegar and sugar for a dip (cho-gochujang), or glaze grilled meat.
Keep it in the fridge after opening; it lasts a long time but darkens over time.

explained.title: Cushion compact, explained: the Korean invention that changed makeup
explained.sub: Why a sponge-in-a-compact became a global format.
points: Liquid foundation soaked into a sponge inside a compact, applied with a puff. Popularised by Korean brands in the late 2000s.
Light, natural coverage that is quick to apply and easy to touch up on the go.
Glow (dewy), semi-matte and matte. Korean ranges often run lighter, so shade range matters for buyers.
Most cushions sell refills, which is better value and a reason customers stay with a brand.

explained.title: Gim, explained: Korean seaweed beyond the snack pack
explained.sub: Seasoned laver is one of Korea's biggest food exports.
points: Gim is dried laver seaweed. Roasted with oil and salt it becomes seasoned gim, eaten with rice in Korea every day.
Snack packs, large sheets for gimbap (unseasoned), seaweed chips (bugak) and flavoured snacks.
Wrap a bite of rice in a small sheet, or crumble it over rice and noodles.
Gimbap needs unseasoned sheets; seasoned snack gim will not roll properly.

explained.title: Sun sticks, explained: why Koreans reapply SPF this way
explained.sub: A solid sunscreen format that is easy to carry and reapply.
points: Sunscreen in a solid stick, swiped on like a balm. Popular for reapplying over makeup.
Korean shoppers reapply sunscreen during the day, and a stick does not mess up makeup or hands.
Korea uses SPF plus PA+ to PA++++ for UVA protection. More plus signs = more UVA protection.
Sunscreen is regulated as a drug in the US and has extra rules in many markets. Check before importing.

explained.title: Tteokbokki, explained: Korea's favourite street food
explained.sub: Chewy rice cakes in a sweet-spicy sauce, now sold frozen worldwide.
points: Cylinder rice cakes simmered in a gochujang-based sauce, often with fish cake and boiled egg.
Classic red, rose (cream and chilli), black-bean (jjajang) and soy-sauce royal court style.
Rice cakes are chewier; wheat cakes are softer and soak up sauce. Packs say which.
Frozen and shelf-stable kits travel well; fresh rice cakes harden fast, so soak them before cooking.

explained.title: Niacinamide, explained: the K-beauty all-rounder
explained.sub: Why it shows up in toners, serums and creams across Korea.
points: A form of vitamin B3, water-soluble and easy to combine with other ingredients.
Korean brands use it in brightening and tone-evening products; in Korea it is a registered functional ingredient for brightening.
Products range widely. Higher is not always better: some skin reacts to very high concentrations.
Look for the functional-cosmetic mark on Korean packaging if you want a formula reviewed for that claim.

explained.title: Heartleaf, explained: the plant behind K-beauty's calming toners
explained.sub: A Korean favourite for oily and breakout-prone skin.
points: Houttuynia cordata, called heartleaf for its shape and eoseongcho in Korean.
Mostly in toners, pads and serums positioned for calming and oil control.
Heartleaf toners became viral exports, putting the ingredient on shelves far from Korea.
Check the percentage on the front and where it appears in the ingredient list.

explained.title: Yakgwa, explained: the old Korean sweet that went viral
explained.sub: A traditional honey cookie younger Koreans rediscovered.
points: A deep-fried cookie of wheat flour, sesame oil and honey, soaked in syrup. Traditionally made for holidays and rites.
Younger Koreans rediscovered it as a 'retro' dessert, and cafés added it to cookies, cakes and drinks.
Dense, sweet and chewy with ginger and honey notes. Best with tea or coffee.
Mini sizes and individually wrapped packs ship and sell better than large traditional ones.

explained.title: Ceramide, explained: why Korean moisturisers talk about the skin barrier
explained.sub: The 'barrier' trend in Korea starts here.
points: Ceramides are lipids naturally found in the outer layer of skin, between skin cells.
Korean marketing focuses on 'barrier' care: keeping that outer layer intact so skin holds moisture.
Moisturisers, body lotions and creams for dry or sensitive skin, often with cholesterol and fatty acids.
Look for named ceramides (like ceramide NP) in the ingredient list rather than just 'barrier' on the front.

explained.title: Nurungji, explained: Korea's crispy scorched rice
explained.sub: From the bottom of the pot to a packaged snack and comfort food.
points: The crust of rice that toasts at the bottom of the pot, dried into crispy sheets.
As a crunchy snack, or boiled in water into a soft, nutty porridge (sungnyung).
Simple ingredients, long shelf life and a comforting, familiar taste for Koreans abroad.
Check for plain rice versions versus sweetened snack versions; they are used differently.

explained.title: Lip tints, explained: the Korean lip look
explained.sub: Why Korean lip products stain instead of sitting on top.
points: A lightweight liquid or gel that stains the lips with colour, made popular by Korean makeup brands.
A soft, blurred gradient that is deeper in the centre of the lips, known in Korea as gradient lips.
Water, glossy (glass) and velvet tints. Glossy and water tints feel lightest.
Tints can stain for hours; use an oil-based cleanser to remove them fully.

explained.title: Konjac jelly, explained: Korea's low-calorie snack
explained.sub: Why drinkable jelly pouches fill Korean convenience stores.
points: Jelly made from konjac, a root high in fibre, usually sold as a drinkable pouch.
It fits Korea's low-calorie and 'healthy pleasure' snack trend.
Chill it and drink straight from the pouch. Many brands suggest freezing it too.
Some markets restrict small, firm konjac jelly cups because of choking risk; drinkable pouches are a different format. Importers should check local rules.

buysmart.title: How to tell real K-beauty from fakes
buysmart.sub: Counterfeits are common on marketplaces. Five checks before you buy.
points: Buy from the brand's official store
Most Korean brands list their official stores on Amazon, other marketplaces and their own websites. Start there.
Big discounts on viral products, far below the brand's own price, are a common warning sign.
Fakes often have blurry print, wrong fonts, misaligned labels or missing Korean text and batch codes.
Different smell, colour or texture from what you know is a red flag. Stop using it and report the seller.

buysmart.title: Why K-beauty costs more abroad than in Korea
buysmart.sub: The same product can be cheaper in Seoul. Here is where the difference comes from.
points: Freight, duties, taxes and compliance work all add to the shelf price abroad.
Korean prices you see online are often sale prices from big events like Olive Young sales.
Export versions sometimes come in different sizes or sets, so compare price per ml, not per item.
Compare the same size at the brand's regular Korean price, then add realistic shipping and tax.

buysmart.title: Your Olive Young shopping list for Seoul
buysmart.sub: How to shop Korea's biggest beauty store like a local.
points: Olive Young runs big sales several times a year and a member sale every month. Check before your trip.
Products with Olive Young Awards labels are best-sellers chosen from Korean sales and reviews.
Many products and sets are sold only in Korea; they make the best souvenirs and gifts.
Tourists can often get tax back at the counter above a minimum spend. Bring your passport.

buysmart.title: How to read a Korean cosmetics label
buysmart.sub: Four things on the box that tell you what you are buying.
points: Korean packaging lists all ingredients in descending order of amount, under 전성분.
Products reviewed in Korea for brightening, anti-wrinkle or sun protection carry 기능성화장품 on the box.
Look for the manufacturing or expiry date and the batch number (제조번호).
A small open-jar icon with a number (like 12M) shows how many months to use it after opening.

buysmart.title: Where Koreans buy K-food online and in person
buysmart.sub: And what that means if you are sourcing abroad.
points: Koreans buy a large share of groceries online with next-morning delivery, through Coupang, Kurly and Naver.
New snacks, ramyeon and drinks often launch first in convenience stores like CU and GS25.
E-mart, Homeplus and Lotte Mart sell family-size staples and private-label foods.
A product trending in Korean convenience stores is an early signal; watch it before it reaches export shelves.

buysmart.title: Shipping K-food abroad: what travels well
buysmart.sub: Not every Korean food survives export. Here is what does.
points: Dried, shelf-stable and retort products: ramyeon, gim, sauces in sealed packs, snacks and teas.
Kimchi, fresh rice cakes and frozen gimbap need refrigerated or frozen shipping, which costs more.
Meat extracts, certain additives and labels can block imports in some markets. Check before ordering.
Most markets require local-language labels, ingredients and allergens. Plan this with your supplier.

buysmart.title: Buying K-beauty on Amazon: smart checks
buysmart.sub: Most K-beauty sales abroad happen here. Shop it carefully.
points: Look for 'Sold by' the brand or an authorised store. Official brand stores are usually linked from the brand name.
Read recent reviews and photos. Complaints about smell or texture changes can mean old or fake stock.
Check the expiry or manufacturing date when it arrives, especially for sunscreens and actives.
Use the Korean name to check what Koreans pay and say about it before paying a big markup.

buysmart.title: Korean gift sets: what to buy for holidays
buysmart.sub: Koreans give gift sets for Chuseok and Seollal. Here is what is inside.
points: Spam, tuna and cooking oil sets, fruit, Korean beef and red ginseng are traditional holiday gifts.
Skincare and hair-care sets are popular, practical gifts at every price point.
Sets fill stores about two to three weeks before each holiday.
Korean gift-set formats often inspire seasonal sets abroad; watch them before your holiday season.

buysmart.title: Sunscreen from Korea: what to know before you import
buysmart.sub: K-sunscreen is hugely popular, and heavily regulated abroad.
points: Korean sunscreens are known for light textures that feel like moisturiser.
In the US, sunscreen is an over-the-counter drug with its own rules and approved filters.
Some UV filters used in Korea are not approved in every market. Check each product's filters.
Selling a sunscreen abroad without meeting local rules risks listings being removed. Check first.

buysmart.title: How to find the Korean version of a product
buysmart.sub: Search like a Korean to see real reviews and real prices.
points: Brands print the Korean product name on the box and on their Korean websites.
Naver is Korea's main search engine and shopping guide. Search the Korean name there.
Korean beauty review apps and Olive Young reviews show what Korean shoppers think.
Browser translation is good enough to read reviews and compare prices.

buysmart.title: Seoul food souvenirs that travel well
buysmart.sub: What to bring home from a Korean supermarket.
points: Honey butter chips, seaweed snacks and yakgwa are favourites and pack easily.
Buy a few you cannot get at home: convenience stores often have limited flavours.
Gochujang and doenjang in sealed tubs travel well in checked luggage.
Meat products and some fresh foods are not allowed into many countries. Check before you pack.

buysmart.title: Starting to sell K-beauty: three paths
buysmart.sub: How small sellers abroad usually begin.
points: Licensed distributors in your market are the simplest start, with local labels and compliance handled.
Many Korean brands have export teams; expect minimum orders and paperwork.
Korean OEM and ODM makers produce under your brand. More control, more work.
Check what is rising in Korea now, and which categories your market's rules make easier.

guides.title: The Korean 10-step routine, honestly explained
guides.sub: Most Koreans don't do ten steps. Here is what the routine really is.
points: It's a menu, not a rule
The famous '10 steps' is a list of options. Most Koreans pick four or five depending on skin and season.
Cleanser, toner, moisturiser and sunscreen in the morning are what almost everyone does.
Thin, watery layers first, thicker creams last, so each one absorbs.
Add one new product at a time so you know what works for your skin.

guides.title: Double cleansing: why Koreans wash twice
guides.sub: Oil first, water second. The reason is simple.
points: A cleansing oil or balm dissolves sunscreen and makeup.
A gentle foam or gel removes what is left.
Anyone wearing sunscreen or makeup. On bare-skin days, one wash is enough.
Squeaky-clean skin usually means over-cleansed skin.

guides.title: Essence vs serum vs ampoule
guides.sub: Three Korean product names that confuse everyone.
points: Light and watery, used right after toner to hydrate.
More concentrated, usually built around one goal like brightening or calming.
The most concentrated, often used for a short boost.
Brands use the names loosely. Read the ingredients, not the label.

guides.title: Sheet masks: how Koreans actually use them
guides.sub: A Korean staple that is cheap, quick and everywhere.
points: After cleansing and toner, for 10 to 20 minutes.
Leaving a mask on until it dries can pull moisture back out.
Pat in the leftover essence, then apply moisturiser.
Low price, clear promise, and easy to try many brands.

guides.title: Glass skin, explained
guides.sub: The Korean look of clear, smooth, glowing skin.
points: Skin that looks smooth and reflects light, like glass.
Hydration layers, gentle exfoliation and barrier care over time.
Dewy cushions and highlighters create the look on the surface.
Filters and lighting do a lot in photos. Healthy skin is the goal.

guides.title: Korean sunscreen textures, explained
guides.sub: Why people abroad hunt for Korean SPF.
points: Many feel like a light moisturiser rather than a thick paste.
Some add a soft brightening tint.
Korea sells both; mineral ones can leave more white cast.
UV filters allowed in Korea are not always allowed elsewhere.

guides.title: How Korea makes 'functional cosmetics'
guides.sub: A Korean label that means a claim was reviewed.
points: Products for brightening, wrinkles, sun protection and some other claims are reviewed in Korea.
Look for 기능성화장품 printed on the box.
It shows the claim was checked, not just marketing words.
It is a useful signal when comparing Korean formulas.

guides.title: Hanbang: Korean herbal beauty
guides.sub: Ginseng, rice and herbs in modern skincare.
points: Skincare inspired by traditional Korean herbal medicine.
Ginseng, rice, licorice root and fermented herbs.
Often premium, with rich textures and gold or red packaging.
Younger brands use the same ingredients in simple, modern formulas.

guides.title: Rice in Korean skincare
guides.sub: An old ingredient with a new following.
points: Rice water has long been used in Korean households for washing.
Toners, cleansers and masks with rice extract or ferment.
Simple, familiar and positioned for soft, even-looking skin.
Check where rice appears in the ingredient list.

guides.title: Fermented skincare, explained
guides.sub: Why Korean labels love the word 'ferment'.
points: Ingredients processed with yeast or bacteria, like in food fermentation.
A food culture of kimchi and soy sauce made the idea feel natural.
Lighter, more absorbable textures and gentle results.
Look for names like galactomyces or bifida ferment.

guides.title: Korean men's skincare
guides.sub: Korea has one of the world's most active men's grooming markets.
points: Many men use one product that works as toner, essence and lotion.
Sunscreen and tinted BB creams are common for men too.
Cleanse, all-in-one, sunscreen is a typical routine.
Clear, simple products sell best to new male customers.

guides.title: Scalp care: Korea's next big category
guides.sub: Koreans treat the scalp like facial skin.
points: Hair thinning worries and long hours under stress pushed demand.
Scalp scalers, tonics, serums and gentle shampoos.
Seoul has salons dedicated to scalp care.
Scalp care is growing beyond Korea; watch Korean launches.

guides.title: Korean body care is booming
guides.sub: Not just faces anymore.
points: Face-style actives like niacinamide in body products.
Exfoliating towels and scrubs are a Korean bathhouse tradition.
Perfumed body lotions and washes sell strongly.
Body care is less crowded than face care abroad.

guides.title: The Korean bathhouse (jjimjilbang)
guides.sub: A Korean ritual that shaped its beauty culture.
points: Public bathhouses with hot pools, saunas and sleeping halls.
Full-body exfoliation with a rough towel is a classic experience.
Baked eggs and sweet rice drinks are part of the ritual.
It explains Korea's love of exfoliation and body care.

guides.title: Seoul's beauty neighbourhoods
guides.sub: Where to shop K-beauty in Seoul.
points: Dense with brand stores and tourist-friendly shops.
Pop-ups and new brand flagships, popular with young Koreans.
Many stores offer tax refunds for tourists above a minimum spend.

guides.title: Pop-up stores: how Korean brands launch
guides.sub: Seoul tests new products in short-term shops.
points: Temporary shops that open for days or weeks.
To get feedback, photos and buzz before wider launches.
Seongsu and the Yeouido area host many pop-ups.
Products that draw queues often become export hits.

guides.title: Korea's daily delivery culture
guides.sub: Order tonight, receive by morning.
points: Groceries ordered at night arrive before breakfast.
Many online orders arrive the next day.
Online-first brands can grow fast without stores.
Korean online rankings move quickly and are a good trend signal.

guides.title: Korean convenience stores, explained
guides.sub: Where new snacks and drinks launch first.
points: Convenience stores are on almost every street.
New ramyeon, snacks and drinks often debut here.
Limited editions with characters and celebrities sell out fast.
A convenience-store hit is often next year's export trend.

guides.title: Kimchi, explained
guides.sub: More than one dish: a whole family of fermented vegetables.
points: Napa cabbage, radish cubes, cucumber and more.
Kimchi gets sourer as it ferments; older kimchi is used for stews.
As a side dish with almost every meal.
Check if it contains fish sauce or shrimp if you need it vegan.

guides.title: Korean banchan, explained
guides.sub: The small side dishes on every Korean table.
points: Small shared dishes served with rice.
Seasoned spinach, bean sprouts, braised potatoes and kimchi.
At many restaurants, side dishes are refilled free.
Packaged banchan is a growing grocery category.

guides.title: Korean ramyeon, explained
guides.sub: Why Korean instant noodles are a category of their own.
points: Korean ramyeon tends to be spicier and chewier than other instant noodles.
With egg, green onion and sometimes cheese.
Soup ramyeon, stir-fried noodles and cold noodles.
Limited flavours launch often; watch Korean convenience stores.

guides.title: Korean fried chicken, explained
guides.sub: Double-fried, crispy and everywhere in Korea.
points: Frying twice makes a thin, crisp skin.
Chicken with beer is a Korean night-out classic.
Korean fried-chicken sauces sell well in retail.

guides.title: Korean BBQ at home
guides.sub: The basics of the Korean grill table.
points: Pork belly and marinated beef are the classics.
Lettuce with meat, garlic and ssamjang sauce.
Kimchi and banchan grill or sit alongside.
Marinades and ssamjang are easy entry products.

guides.title: Ssamjang and doenjang, explained
guides.sub: The soybean pastes behind Korean flavour.
points: A fermented soybean paste for stews and soups.
Doenjang mixed with gochujang and seasonings, for wraps.

guides.title: Korean street food guide
guides.sub: What to try at a Seoul market.
points: A sweet pancake filled with brown sugar and nuts.
Fish cake skewers in hot broth.
A small bread with a whole egg inside.

guides.title: Korean cafe culture
guides.sub: Why Seoul has so many cafes.
points: Seoul has a cafe on almost every block.
Cakes, bingsu and trendy pastries drive visits.
Cafes double as study and meeting spaces.
Cafe dessert trends often become packaged snacks.

guides.title: Bingsu, explained
guides.sub: Korea's shaved-ice dessert.
points: Finely shaved ice or milk ice with toppings.
Patbingsu with sweet red beans and rice cakes.
A summer favourite, but cafes serve it all year.

guides.title: Korean tea beyond green tea
guides.sub: Grain and fruit teas Koreans drink daily.
points: Roasted barley tea is a common table drink.
Yuja marmalade mixed with hot water.
Caffeine-free grain teas travel and sell well.

guides.title: Korean snacks that travel well
guides.sub: Shelf-stable favourites for buyers.
points: Check allergen labels for each market.

guides.title: Hangwa: traditional Korean sweets
guides.sub: Old-style confections having a revival.
points: Traditional sweets made with grains, honey and fruit.
Honey cookies that went viral with younger Koreans.
Modern packaging makes them good gift products.

guides.title: Korean holiday food: Seollal and Chuseok
guides.sub: What Koreans eat at their biggest holidays.
points: Rice-cake soup for the new year.
Holiday gift sets fill stores weeks ahead.
Holiday timing shapes Korean demand and shipping.

guides.title: Korean dosirak, explained
guides.sub: The Korean lunch box.
points: Rice with several side dishes in one box.
Affordable boxed meals are a big category.
Home-packed boxes for school and work.
Frozen and ready meals are a growing export.

guides.title: Korean frozen food boom
guides.sub: Why Korean frozen foods are spreading abroad.
points: Mandu are among the best-known exports.
Frozen gimbap became a viral overseas hit.
Cold chain adds cost; plan it early.

guides.title: Mandu, explained
guides.sub: Korean dumplings.
points: Dumplings filled with meat, tofu, vegetables or kimchi.
Steamed, pan-fried, boiled or in soup.
Frozen mandu is a proven export category.

guides.title: Japchae, explained
guides.sub: Glass noodles stir-fried with vegetables.
points: Sweet potato starch noodles with vegetables and soy sauce.
Sweet potato noodles are naturally gluten-free; check sauces.

guides.title: Bibimbap, explained
guides.sub: Korea's mixed rice bowl.
points: Rice topped with vegetables, egg and gochujang.
Dolsot bibimbap gets a crispy rice crust.
A good first Korean dish for newcomers.

guides.title: Korean soups and stews
guides.sub: Comfort food Koreans eat all year.
points: Stew kits and pastes are simple export products.

guides.title: Korean drinking culture basics
guides.sub: Soju, makgeolli and etiquette.
points: Korea's most popular spirit, usually drunk in small glasses.
A milky rice wine, often with pancakes.
Pour for others, not yourself; turn away from elders when drinking.
Flavoured soju is a big export category.

guides.title: Hangover culture in Korea
guides.sub: Korea has a whole market for the morning after.
points: Bean-sprout soup and pollack soup are classics.
After-work drinking is part of work culture.
Hangover drinks are a growing export curiosity.

guides.title: Korean health food trends
guides.sub: What health-minded Koreans buy.
points: Zero-sugar drinks and snacks are everywhere.
Korean wellness brands are expanding abroad.

guides.title: Red ginseng, explained
guides.sub: Korea's most famous health product.
points: Ginseng that is steamed and dried, turning red.
A top holiday gift in Korea.
Health-claim rules differ by country; check before importing.

guides.title: Korean tteok (rice cakes), explained
guides.sub: Rice cakes beyond tteokbokki.
points: Rice cakes coated in roasted soybean powder.
Fresh tteok hardens fast; frozen travels better.

guides.title: Korean pancakes (jeon), explained
guides.sub: Savoury pancakes for rainy days and holidays.
points: Koreans eat jeon with makgeolli when it rains.
Pancake mix is an easy retail product.

guides.title: How Koreans shop for skincare
guides.sub: Reviews, rankings and ingredient apps.
points: Koreans check ingredient ratings in apps before buying.
Store and app rankings drive many purchases.
Free samples and minis are expected.
Clear ingredient lists win trust in Korea.

guides.title: Korean beauty awards, explained
guides.sub: Why award labels sell products in Korea.
points: Stores like Olive Young pick yearly winners from sales and reviews.
Winners get special labels in stores.
Shoppers trust real sales over ads.
Award winners are lower-risk import picks.

guides.title: K-beauty for sensitive skin
guides.sub: How Korean brands talk to sensitive skin.
points: Minimal formulas are a selling point.
Look for dermatologist or sensitive-skin test labels.

guides.title: Acne care, the Korean way
guides.sub: Gentle routines and patches.
points: Hydrocolloid patches are a Korean staple.
Korean routines avoid harsh, drying products.

guides.title: Pimple patches, explained
guides.sub: Small stickers that went global from Korea.
points: Hydrocolloid stickers placed over a spot.
They cover the spot and keep hands away.
Clear day patches and thicker night patches.

guides.title: Lip care, Korean style
guides.sub: Lip masks, balms and tints.
points: Thick overnight lip treatments are a Korean hit.
Moisture plus a hint of colour.
Lip products are easy, low-cost entry items.

guides.title: Korean eye makeup trends
guides.sub: Soft, natural and youthful.
points: Highlighting the small fold under the eyes.
Straight, natural brows rather than sharp arches.
Small palettes with soft tones sell widely.

guides.title: Korean hair care, explained
guides.sub: Treatments, oils and salon culture.
points: Rinse-off treatments after shampoo are common.
Light oils for shine and ends.
Perms and colour are everyday services.
Korean salon brands are expanding retail lines.

guides.title: Korean perfume and scent trends
guides.sub: Soft, clean scents lead in Korea.
points: Light, soapy and clean fragrances are popular.
Korean niche perfume houses are growing.
Scent is personal; sample sets help sales.

guides.title: Korean nail trends
guides.sub: Detailed, cute and seasonal nails.
points: Korean press-on gel nails are a big export.
Designs change with seasons and holidays.
Press-ons are light, cheap to ship and trendy.

guides.title: Clinic culture in Seoul
guides.sub: Why skin clinics are everywhere in Korea.
points: Skin clinics are a normal part of beauty in Korea.
Clinic ingredients often move into everyday products.
Many visitors book treatments in Seoul.
Choose licensed clinics and ask about aftercare.

guides.title: K-beauty packaging, explained
guides.sub: Why Korean packaging looks the way it does.
points: Characters and fun shapes attract young buyers.
Refill packs reduce waste and cost.
Local labels must cover the Korean text abroad.

guides.title: Korean beauty on a budget
guides.sub: Affordable brands Koreans love.
points: Koreans love good value, called gasungbi.
Many best-sellers are affordable drugstore lines.
Big retailer sales cut prices further.
Value brands travel well to price-sensitive markets.

guides.title: Korean wellness drinks

points: Powdered kombucha became a Korean hit.
Powder sticks are light and easy to ship.
